image_description:
## 1. Chart type
A **composite visualization** with:
- a **dot plot / stacked dot chart** on top
- a **vertical bar chart** on the bottom

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Two vertically stacked panels** showing different measures over time.
- The **top panel** uses **stacking of dots** within each year to show counts.
- The **bottom panel** uses **bars by year** and **color highlighting** for selected disasters.
- No faceting or small multiples are used.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year (top chart) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Number of hurricanes making landfall in the continental United States | Quantitative | Stacked dots / vertical count of dots per year |
| Year (bottom chart) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Total cost of major natural disasters (for disasters causing more than $1 billion in losses) | Quantitative | Bar height / position on y-axis |
| Selected disaster/event name (e.g., Hurricane Katrina, Hurricane Harvey, Hurricane Maria, Hurricane Irma, California wildfires) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels/annotations |
| Highlighted disaster bars vs. other years | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (dark red for highlighted events, light pink for others) |

comments.raw_comment: For this assignment, students were asked to pick a graph that interested them and interpret it in as many ways as possible. This graph first caught my eye because of its relevance to my real life and how it has and will impact me in the years to come/years past. What I notice about this graph is that from the 1980s-2000 hurricanes and other natural disasters didn’t happen very often and were not nearly as costly. I also noticed that the two highest years, cost wise, are 2005 and 2018. In 2018, there were four major natural disasters that cost millions of dollars. While in 2005, there was one major disaster that was so devastating it cost about ¾ of what 2018 had brought. These pieces of data show me that in more recent times natural disasters have been increasing at a concerning rate and this could potentially be due to human errors and other factors. Secondly, what I wonder from this graph is exactly why these natural disasters have increased so much in recent years. I can’t think of any major reasons that these disasters would sky rocket so high in 2018. Another thing that I can wonder from this graph is why Hurricane Katrina was so costly. I wasn’t born yet for this hurricane, so I’m not exactly sure the damage it caused. Lastly, I also am wondering if in 2019 and all the years after that the natural disaster rate will be as high as it was in 2018. I’m not sure if this is easily predictable, but I believe it can be solved. (cont in next post)
